abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a rapidly progressing neurodegenerative disorder that selectively affects motor neurons. The median survival time after diagnosis is 2 to 5 years. Oxidative stress (OS), driven mainly by reactive oxygen species (ROS), plays a central role in motor neuron (MN) degeneration. In this narrative review, we analyse the pathogenic role of SOD1 variants and their contribution to OS in ALS. SOD1 mutations alter the Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase enzyme, thereby promoting oxidative damage and triggering neuroinflammatory cascades via the MAPK, NF-κB and Nrf2/ARE signalling pathways. We also discuss emerging proteomic and machine-learning biomarkers, as well as the current therapeutic landscape. Riluzole and edaravone are approved treatments, while AMX0035 was approved in 2022 but withdrawn in 2024. Masitinib and EPI-589 remain investigational. In the realm of genetic therapies, the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen received accelerated FDA approval in 2023 for SOD1-ALS, primarily due to its ability to reduce plasma neurofilament light chain levels. However, the clinical benefit remains modest. RNA interference has reached human trials, while CRISPR/Cas9 remains in the preclinical stage. Both approaches have shown promising results in experimental models. Further research into ALS pathogenesis is needed to develop treatments that integrate antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and gene-editing strategies.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) remains a major global health problem. Functional cure is defined as sustained hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroclearance with undetectable HBV DNA 24 weeks after cessation of therapy. It has emerged as a clinically meaningful endpoint, associated with regression of liver fibrosis, reduced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk, and a lower treatment burden. However, current CHB therapies, including nucleos(t)ide analogues (NUCs) and pegylated interferon-α (Peg-IFNα), rarely lead to functional cure despite adequate viral suppression, leading to a notable portion of patients remaining at risk for adverse liver-related outcomes, including hepatic decompensation and HCC. Hence, novel therapeutic agents are aimed at accelerating towards functional cure. They are categorized as virus-targeting and immunomodulatory therapies.
METHODS: This review summarizes the clinical evidence for emerging therapies aimed at acheiving functional cure, with a particular focus on RNA-targeting therapies. It also discusses practical considerations relevant to treatment selection.
RESULTS: Among these novel therapies, RNA-targeting therapies are currently the most promising, with bepirovirsen (an unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide) standing out as the only agent completed in Phase III study showing efficacious results. Combination regimens that use RNA-targeting therapies as backbone are increasingly pursued, leveraging potential synergistic effects to achieve higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance.
CONCLUSION: RNA-targetting therapies and combination regimens offer promising approaches in attaining functional cure in CHB. Further research should emphasize on the long-term efficacy and safety for these novel agents.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.

abstract: mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines are detectable in human blood after vaccination, but platform-specific differences in systemic persistence and transcript integrity remain poorly defined. We analyzed serial blood samples from 73 participants receiving Moderna mRNA-1273 (three formulations), Pfizer/BioNTech BNT162b2, or an investigational receptor-binding domain (RBD) mRNA vaccine (three different doses). Using droplet digital polymerase chain reaction (ddPCR) assays, we quantified total and long-range linked ("intact") vaccine mRNA, and we measured vaccine-specific ionizable lipids by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Across platforms, mRNA decay was fastest for mRNA-1273, intermediate for BNT162b2, and slowest for the RBD vaccine, with ionizable lipid decay following the same rank order. Notably, intact spike mRNA declined 2-fold faster after mRNA-1273 than BNT162b2 vaccination. Kinetics modeling revealed platform-dependent coupling of mRNA and lipid kinetics: intact mRNA tracked closely with SM-102 for mRNA-1273, whereas ALC-0315 persisted longer than intact mRNA for BNT162b2. A ten-fragment linkage ddPCR panel spanning the spike transcript showed lower linkage toward 3'-proximal regions that mirrored the administered mRNA-1273 formulation. Together, these data provide a quantitative framework for benchmarking mRNA-LNP platform kinetics and transcript integrity in humans.

abstract: Chronic lung diseases arise from complex interactions between environmental exposures and host genetic factors. However, these interactions are not fully understood, and despite decades of study, effective curative therapies remain unavailable for many patients. Recent breakthroughs in therapeutic gene-editing have become a reality for some inherited blood diseases and are a promising approach for monogenic lung diseases. Early-phase clinical studies are now ongoing for AATD, primarily through liver-directed editing of hepatocytes to restore circulating functional AAT and for COVID-19 using gene-edited immune cell approaches. However, direct in vivo gene-editing of pulmonary epithelial cells remains largely at the preclinical stage. Expanding this therapeutic pipeline requires overcoming the unique biological barriers of the lung and developing human-specific models that faithfully recapitulate human disease mechanisms. Advances in gene-editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9 systems, base and prime editors, and emerging compact nucleases, have increased the feasibility of precise genomic correction. However, safe and efficient delivery directly to the lung remains a major unmet challenge due to mucus, surfactant, epithelial tight junctions, and innate immune surveillance. Delivery systems such as engineered AAVs, lentiviral vectors, selective organ targeting lipid nanoparticles and aerosolizable formulations like nebulised or dry powder nanoparticles are beginning to address these obstacles. In parallel, human preclinical models have evolved from traditional cell lines to more sophisticated platforms such as iPSC-derived airway and alveolar cells, organoids, precision-cut lung slices, air-liquid interface cultures, organ-on-a-chip devices, and patient-derived primary cells. These models enable mechanistic interrogation, variant-specific functional assessment, and preclinical evaluation of gene-editing strategies with increased physiological relevance. In this review, we detail current and emerging gene-editing tools, delivery strategies, and human-relevant disease models. We highlight key translational barriers and discuss how advanced human models combined with improved delivery technologies can accelerate the development of safe and effective gene-editing therapeutics for chronic respiratory disease.

abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases remain largely untreatable at the disease-modifying level, with currently approved therapies providing primarily symptomatic benefits. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality because of its ability to selectively silence disease-associated genes. However, a major obstacle to clinical translation is not the gene-silencing mechanism itself, but the efficient delivery of therapeutic siRNAs to target cells within the central nervous system.This review examines the barriers that limit siRNA-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. We adopt a barrier-oriented framework that follows the sequential challenges encountered during siRNA delivery, including extracellular instability, unfavorable pharmacokinetics, immune recognition, limited transport across the blood-brain barrier, inefficient cellular internalization, and endosomal entrapment. Rather than cataloguing available delivery systems, we evaluate how nanocarrier engineering strategies have been developed to address these barriers and assess their impact on delivery. Evidence from Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and Huntington's disease is synthesized to distinguish shared limitations from disease-specific challenges and to evaluate the translational performance of lipid-based nanoparticles, polymeric nanocarriers, engineered exosomes, and hybrid platforms.Available evidence indicates that delivery platforms can improve specific aspects of siRNA transport but have not consistently overcome the sequential biological barriers required for therapy. Although nanocarrier engineering has enhanced siRNA stability, brain targeting, intracellular trafficking, and gene-silencing efficiency in preclinical models, manufacturing scalability, biological heterogeneity, long-term safety, reproducibility, and regulatory feasibility remain important barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will likely depend on delivery systems that integrate effective brain transport, endosomal escape, controlled intracellular release, and scalable manufacturing within clinical platforms.

title: Why does siRNA delivery still fail in neurodegenerative diseases? Biological barriers, nanocarrier engineering, and future translational directions.

abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

title: In Vivo CRISPR Screen Identifies RPS19 as an Immunotherapy Target in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

title: CAR-NK cell immunotherapy: a comprehensive review of engineering platforms, clinical applications in hematological and solid tumors.

abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is still a global health challenge, as there is no effective treatment due to the inadequacy of conventional experimental platforms for comprehending pathogenic mechanisms and developing therapy. Objectives: This review details the recent progress and clinical utility of next-generation iPSC-derived 3D in vitro systems integrated with microfluidics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, multi-omics readouts, and AI-based machine learning, which are emerging as transformative platforms for recapitulating key ALS pathological hallmarks. Methods: A literature search was performed using PubMed and Web of Science, including only English-language publications. All the published papers collected covered the period from January 2015 to June 2026. Results: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cerebral organoids, assembloids, and organ-on-a-chip technologies are revolutionizing research into ALS by providing a way to model the complex spatial organization, cellular heterogeneity, and neural network dynamics of the human brain. Moreover, recent bioengineering advancements enable the inclusion of functional neurovascular units, the integration of resident immune cells (microglia), and the use of 3D bioprinting to accelerate the functional maturation of age-related phenotypes. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, OMICS, and machine learning improve tools for studying ALS and identifying therapeutic targets. Conclusions: Novel cell culture models may bridge the gap between preclinical animal models and human clinical trials and reduce the duration and costs of translation. Future work is likely to integrate bioprinting with organ-on-chip microfluidics, CRISPR-based genetic editing, and multi-omics readouts to build increasingly faithful, patient-specific ALS models for both basic research and precision therapeutics.

title: Advancing the Translational Pipeline: From In Vivo and In Vitro 2D Models to Next-Generation Cell Culture Models for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Modelling and Drug Discovery.

abstract:
AIM: In vitro air-liquid interface (ALI) cultures of human airway epithelial cells are widely used to study respiratory biology and disease, as they recapitulate key features of the pseudostratified airway epithelium and reduce reliance on animal models and repeated patient biopsies. However, the limited proliferative capacity of primary airway basal cells restricts long-term studies and genome editing. This study aimed to generate stable, immortalised human airway basal cell lines that retain differentiation capacity and support genetic manipulation.
METHODS: Human airway epithelial basal cells from bronchial and nasal origin were immortalised by lentiviral expression of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (hTERT) followed by polyclonal expansion. A panel of cell lines derived from three independent nasal donors was established. Differentiation capacity was assessed in ALI cultures and compared with primary airway epithelial cells. Suitability for genetic manipulation was evaluated using lentiviral overexpression and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene knockout and knock-in strategies.
RESULTS: All immortalised cell lines displayed sustained proliferative capacity and efficiently differentiated into major airway epithelial cell types, including multiciliated and secretory cells. Differentiation patterns and functional characteristics closely resembled those of primary airway epithelial cultures. The cell lines supported efficient lentiviral transduction and CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, enabling stable gene overexpression, targeted gene disruption, and precise genomic modification.
CONCLUSIONS: hTERT-immortalised human airway basal cell lines preserve key features of primary airway epithelium while enabling long-term culture and versatile genome editing. This resource provides a robust platform for airway biology research, disease modelling, and therapeutic development.

title: Immortalisation of human airway epithelial cells for genome editing applications.

abstract: CRISPR/Cas9 enables precision gene editing via homology-directed repair (HDR) for mutation correction and disease modelling. Here we present a customizable T cell single nucleotide variant (SNV) correction platform based on non-viral HDR, previously described in Mamia et al. Precision T Cell Correction Platform for Inborn Errors of Immunity. Molecular Therapy, 2025. To enable reproducible application, we provide a comprehensive, step-by-step 8-day HDR workflow for editing primary T cells, covering CRISPR/Cas9 reagent design, custom genomic editing from start to finish, optimization and validation strategies, on-target detection, and flow cytometric assessment of T cell phenotype and exhaustion. The platform separates locus-specific reagent optimization from a fixed cellular workflow, enabling implementation of new genomic targets without modifying the downstream T cell editing pipeline. Using this workflow, we have achieved up to 80% editing efficiency across multiple loci and donors. We have further optimized the T cell culture platform for PBMC stimulation to promote CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation and proliferation. We validated this culture platform in 33 patients with Inborn Errors of Immunity using flow cytometry and observed that the defined culture conditions maintain low T cell exhaustion and support persistence of memory T cell populations. The protocol was developed under research-grade conditions but supports scalability and transition to preclinical and clinical GMP workflows. Overall, this adaptable platform is a broadly applicable framework for precision T cell engineering across diverse genomic targets offering opportunities for both in vitro disease modeling and therapeutic genome correction.

title: Protocol for non-viral HDR-based CRISPR/Cas9 platform for small custom editing in primary T cells.

abstract: Efficient, biocompatible, and flexible application of CRISPR-Cas9 remains a major challenge in gene therapy. This study addresses a novel formulation method, focusing on organic solvent-free lipid nanoparticles for the efficient delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 components. Therefore, novel stealth lipids comprising the lipid anchor cholesterol hemisuccinate conjugated to poly(2-ethyl-2-oxazoline) (PEtOx) were synthesized and evaluated as a promising in vitro alternative to commercially available poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based lipids. Our study identified PEtOx-lipids as markedly more biocompatible compared to PEG-based analogues (12-fold reduction in cytotoxicity; 99% reduced hemolytic effect) with high efficiency for mRNA gene delivery. We demonstrate successful CRISPR-Cas9 activity ex vivo and efficient uptake of PEtOx nanoparticles by macrophages in vivo (66.5% pos. F4/80+ macrophages). Our data demonstrate that PEtOx-based stealth lipids are a promising alternative to PEG. The resulting LNPs, optimized for fully aqueous manufacturing, address key limitations of current LNP systems, including immunogenicity and the reliance on ethanol-based production processes.

title: Comparative Analysis of Poly(Ethylene Glycol) (PEG) and Poly(2-Ethyl-2-Oxazoline) (PEtOx) for Organic Solvent-Free Lipid Nanoparticle Formulations.

abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4 and CD8 T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus

abstract: ATP1A3-related neurological disorders comprise a rapidly expanding spectrum of rare neurogenetic diseases characterized by remarkable clinical heterogeneity and complex genotype-phenotype relationships. Since the publication of previous comprehensive reviews, the identification of novel ATP1A3-associated phenotypes, refinement of genotype-phenotype correlations, and advances in molecular pathogenesis and precision therapeutic strategies have substantially expanded current understanding of these disorders, highlighting the need for an updated synthesis. This narrative review summarizes recent advances in the clinical spectrum of ATP1A3-related disorders and discusses current insights into genotype-phenotype correlations, molecular mechanisms, and disease pathogenesis. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular consequences of ATP1A3 dysfunction, including impaired Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, disrupted neuronal excitability, altered ion homeostasis, and downstream cellular responses. We further review current symptomatic management and emerging disease-modifying therapeutic strategies, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, viral vector-mediated gene delivery, genome editing technologies, and other precision medicine approaches. Current challenges and future research priorities are also discussed. By integrating recent clinical and experimental evidence, this review provides an updated perspective on ATP1A3-related disorders and aims to facilitate improved disease recognition, mechanistic understanding, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.

abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

title: Potential Therapeutic Applications of Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) in Cancer: Key Observations and Insights.

abstract: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy (SAE) represents the most prevalent neurological complication arising from sepsis, affecting approximately 70% of patients with sepsis and associated with mortality rates reaching up to 70%. Survivors frequently experience persistent cognitive deficits; however, the field currently lacks specific diagnostic biomarkers and targeted therapeutic interventions, with diagnosis primarily established through exclusion criteria. This review critically examines multi-omic investigations of SAE, evaluating whether convergent evidence across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic domains elucidates shared pathophysiological mechanisms and identifying prevailing translational challenges. The synthesis of evidence is structured around three interrelated thematic domains. First, multi-omic analyses have elucidated the initial triggers of neuroinflammation: genomic studies implicate Piezo1-mediated oligodendrocyte ferroptosis and adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, while proteomic data corroborate activation of the reactive oxygen species (ROS)/thioredoxin-interacting protein (TXNIP)/NLRP3 inflammasome axis, collectively indicating that peripheral inflammatory cues converge upon central innate immune pathways. Second, transcriptomic and proteomic findings converge on microglial polarization as a pivotal mediator in SAE progression: single-cell sequencing reveals C1q-dependent synaptic pruning, S100A9 protein expression promotes pro-inflammatory microglial polarization, and metabolomic profiles demonstrate that cyclophilin D (CypD)-regulated redox imbalances modulate the magnitude of glial inflammatory responses. Third, integrative analyses delineate neuronal injury pathways: the NAT10 (N-acetyltransferase 10)/GABA(B) receptor 1 axis is implicated in inhibitory synaptic dysfunction through coordinated transcriptomic and proteomic alterations, while elevated levels of 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid correlate with impaired consciousness, suggesting its potential utility as a prognostic biomarker. Across these domains-initiation, mediation, and injury-multi-omic integration further extends the conceptual framework to encompass systemic regulation via the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Notwithstanding these advances, extant evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional study designs, reliance on single-animal models, and a paucity of rigorous clinical validation. To address these limitations, we propose a three-tiered cascade model-comprising Inflammation Initiation, Glial Mediation, and Neuronal Injury-that synthesizes current findings into a coherent, testable framework. Furthermore, we delineate a methodological roadmap emphasizing longitudinal sampling, multi-center validation, causal inference methodologies, and artificial intelligence-driven data integration. This review endeavors not only to consolidate existing knowledge but also to establish an actionable translational paradigm aimed at advancing SAE research from descriptive characterization toward precision diagnostics and mechanism-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Multi-omics advances in sepsis-associated encephalopathy: from pathogenesis to clinical translation.

abstract: Clinical heterogeneity remains a major challenge across human diseases, where patients with similar genetic backgrounds frequently exhibit striking differences in disease progression, therapeutic response and clinical outcome. Increasing evidence indicates that these differences cannot be explained by genetic variation alone, positioning epigenetic memory as a critical non-genetic determinant of disease behavior. Epigenetic memory refers to the stable yet reversible propagation of transcriptional states through mechanisms including DNA methylation, histone modifications, chromatin accessibility, enhancer dynamics and higher-order chromatin organization. In this review, we synthesize emerging mechanistic and translational evidence demonstrating how epigenetic memory integrates environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, infectious and therapeutic cues into persistent cellular programs that drive inter-patient, intra-tumoral and temporal heterogeneity. We discuss its disease-specific manifestations across cancer, immunological, neurological, and metabolic disorders, with particular emphasis on cellular plasticity, stemness, immune evasion, drug-tolerant persister states and relapse. Furthermore, we highlight recent advances in single-cell and spatial epigenomics, liquid-biopsy-based epigenetic biomarkers, CRISPR-mediated epigenome editing and targeted chromatin therapies that collectively establish epigenetic memory as both a measurable biomarker and a therapeutically actionable vulnerability. By framing epigenetic memory as a dynamic interface between genome and environment, this review provides a unified conceptual framework for understanding disease evolution and advancing precision epigenetic medicine.

title: Epigenetic Memory in Human Diseases: Acquired Chromatin States as Targetable Drivers of Disease Evolution.

abstract: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas (PTCL) comprise a biologically diverse and clinically aggressive family of mature T/NK-cell neoplasms, for which outcomes remain poor in the majority of patients treated with conventional anthracycline-based frontline regimens. Contemporary classifications (WHO-HAEM5 and ICC) increasingly incorporate immunophenotypic and molecular information, underscoring that "PTCL-NOS" is not a single disease but rather a diagnostic umbrella that includes biologically distinct entities and molecular subgroups. Among these are the TBX21- and GATA3-driven PTCL-NOS subsets, the latter associated with inferior survival and a distinctive cytokine/microenvironmental program. These advances, many of which were shaped by long-standing contributions from the Bologna group, support a rational shift from empiric chemotherapy toward mechanism-based and immune-based interventions. CAR-engineered cellular therapies have revolutionized the care of B-cell malignancies, yet translation to PTCL has been delayed by lineage-specific barriers: (i) fratricide during manufacturing when targeting shared T-cell antigens (e.g., CD5, CD7), (ii) the risk of profound and prolonged T-cell aplasia (a markedly less "replaceable" toxicity than B-cell aplasia), and (iii) product contamination by malignant T-cells in autologous platforms. Recent progress in genome editing (CRISPR/Cas9 and base editing), intracellular antigen "blocking" strategies, and alternative effectors (allogeneic "universal" CAR-T, CAR-NK, and iPSC-derived platforms) has begun to address these obstacles at the manufacturing level, while their downstream clinical consequences (e.g., prolonged cytopenias, infectious risk and delayed immune reconstitution) remain incompletely resolved. Early-phase clinical trials now demonstrate clinically meaningful responses for select targets, particularly CD7, CD5, TRBC1 and CD30, for the pan-T targets. However, the strongest efficacy data remain largely derived from T-cell lymphoblastic malignancies (T-ALL/T-LBL), whereas evidence in mature PTCL remains limited and at an earlier stage, with target-specific differences in safety, immune reconstitution and relapse patterns. This review synthesizes the biological rationale for antigen selection in PTCL, the emerging clinical evidence for leading CAR targets, and the engineering strategies most likely to improve the therapeutic index. It also proposes an integrated hematology perspective on how CAR-based therapies might be positioned relative to transplant and evolving targeted agents in relapsed/refractory PTCL.

title: Targeting Peripheral T-Cell Lymphomas with Chimeric Antigen Receptor Therapy: Mechanistic Challenges, Clinical Landscape and Future Engineering Perspectives.

abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Cell-Based Therapies in Retinal Disease.

abstract: Background/Objectives: CRISPR/Cas-dependent base editing enables the precise correction of genomic sequences by direct modification of DNA bases without creating potentially mutagenic DNA double-strand breaks. Base editing is considered a therapeutic approach for rare monogenic disorders or viral infections. However, many variants of base editors suffer from limited specificity because they induce bystander edits within a broad editing window. However, nucleotide substitution is sufficient to correct a mutation or to achieve a therapeutic effect. Methods: PCR, cloning by restriction digest, and ligation were used to create genetic constructs. The editing efficiency was evaluated using NGS. Virus-like particles were produced in HEK293T cells using transient expression. VLPs were visualized by electron microscopy. Results: Using dual base editors that induce C-to-T and A-to-G substitutions, we show that high editing precision can be achieved by engineering the linker between the MmCas12m domain and the deaminase domain of the editor. By testing different linker sequences, we have created high-precision dual base editors with narrowed editing windows that can edit a single nucleotide at a target position with high accuracy. Conclusions: We found that shortening the linker to an acceptable length provides a single-nucleotide substitution in vitro with minimal bystander activity (less than 0.8%), while the high-precision MmCas12m dual base editor retains up to 90% of the editing efficiency of the original base editor. These high-precision base editors will be useful in cases where high precision is required, and editing of adjacent nucleotides is undesirable.

abstract: H3 subtype avian influenza virus (AIV) is one of the most widely distributed and frequently detected low-pathogenicity avian influenza viruses (LPAIVs) in wild birds and poultry worldwide. Wild waterfowl are the natural reservoir of this virus. In recent years, driven by frequent genetic reassortment and continuous evolution, H3 subtype AIV has expanded its host range to include various mammalian species-dogs, cats, horses, seals, pigs (experimental infection), and humans. Among these, the H3N8 subtype shows the broadest cross-species transmissibility, having established sustained transmission lineages in horses and dogs, while also causing sporadic infections in seals and humans. Avian-origin H3N2 canine influenza virus has circulated stably in dog populations across Asia and North America for nearly two decades. Between 2022 and 2023, China reported three human cases of H3N8 subtype AIV infection, one of which was fatal (Guangdong, March 2023), indicating that this virus poses a potential zoonotic transmission risk. Novel triple-reassortant strains, including genotype G25 of H3N8 and H3N3, first detected in chicken flocks in late 2022, have continued to emerge. Their HA genes originate from H3 subtype viruses of wild bird or chicken origin, whereas their internal gene segments are predominantly acquired from H9N2 subtype AIV, resulting in enhanced mammalian adaptability. This review summarizes the global epidemiology of H3 subtype AIV (covering wild birds, poultry, and live poultry markets), its genetic evolution and reassortment patterns, and the molecular mechanisms underlying cross-species transmission. This review particularly highlights the regulatory roles of key amino acid mutations-such as PB2-D701N, M1-M192V, and HA-Q226L/G228S-in receptor binding preference, polymerase activity, and pathogenicity. This review also summarizes recent advances in detection techniques (multiplex RT-PCR, quantum dot-based immunochromatographic strips, RT-RAA, and CRISPR-Cas13a) and vaccine development (inactivated, adenovirus-vectored, and mRNA vaccines). Key prevention and control challenges-including covert circulation, surveillance gaps, and limited subtyping diagnostic capacity at primary laboratories-are also discussed. This review proposes that H3 subtype AIV should be recognized as a potential zoonotic threat warranting continued surveillance, although no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission has been documented to date. Better understanding of cross-species mechanisms, stronger surveillance and early warning, and evidence-based control strategies are needed to inform future risk assessment.

abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is characterized by degeneration of striatal medium spiny neurons (MSNs), yet the human-specific regulatory mechanisms that contribute to neuronal vulnerability remain poorly understood. Here, we identify HD-LINC (LINC01139), a human-specific long intergenic noncoding RNA selectively induced in symptomatic HD patient-derived MSNs (HD-MSNs) and human HD caudate. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in HD-MSNs revealed that HD-LINC was enriched in a symptomatic HD neuronal state associated with lipid metabolic and protein clearance regulation, while not observed in non-degenerative reprogrammed MSNs derived from pre-manifest HD individuals. Reducing HD-LINC attenuated mutant HTT aggregation, dystrophic neurites, DNA damage, and neuronal death, whereas HD-LINC overexpression exacerbated these phenotypes. Transcriptomic and lipidomic analyses further implicated HD-LINC in neuronal lipid regulation. We found that HD-MSNs exhibited aberrant accumulation of enlarged, low-mobility lipid droplets (LDs) within neurites, a previously unrecognized phenotype in patient-derived neurons. Critically, increased lipid peroxidation was observed within LD-enriched dystrophic neurites in HD-MSNs. HD-LINC knockdown cleared neuritic LD accumulation, restored soma-enriched LD distribution, and reduced lipid peroxidation. Finally, we developed antisense oligonucleotides that effectively reduced HD-LINC and reversed HD-LINC-associated phenotypes, nominating HD-LINC lowering as a potential therapeutic strategy in HD. These results identify HD-LINC as a human-specific regulator of neuronal LD spatial organization, lipid peroxidation, and neuronal degeneration in HD. They further reveal dysregulated neuritic LD accumulation driven by HD-LINC, and highlight lincRNA-mediated lipid dysregulation as a significant contributor to neuronal vulnerability to degeneration.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: There is evidence for the protective effects of antibodies targeting non-structural protein 1 (NS1) of Zika virus (ZIKV); however, effective vaccines against ZIKV remain lacking.
METHODS: In this study, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-encapsulated mRNA vaccines were designed based on the envelope domain III (EDIII) and NS1 sequences of the ZIKV FSS13025 strain, while protective efficacy was evaluated in a murine model using a ZIKV isolate obtained from Zhejiang Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Zhejiang CDC).
RESULTS: The vaccines were evaluated for key quality attributes-including particle size, polydispersity index (PDI), and encapsulation efficiency-as well as immunogenicity and protective efficacy. Both monovalent vaccine components exhibited uniform particle sizes (PDI < 0.2) and high encapsulation efficiencies (≥80%) and induced high levels of antigen-specific antibodies in mice in a dose-dependent manner. The EDIII mRNA vaccine elicited moderate ZIKV-neutralizing antibody titers as measured by PRNT50, whereas the NS1 vaccine did not induce detectable neutralizing antibodies. Both bicomponent (EDIII + NS1) mRNA vaccines induced a Th1-biased cellular immune response in mouse splenocytes, with significantly greater IFN-γ production compared with either monovalent vaccine. In viral challenge experiments using 1 × 105 PFU ZIKV (Zhejiang CDC isolate, intraperitoneal), the bicomponent vaccine provided complete protection, with 100% survival across all dose groups. In contrast, the EDIII and NS1 monovalent vaccines showed partial protection: mortality was observed in the 20 μg dose groups and exceeded 50% in the 10 μg dose groups.
CONCLUSIONS: These results demonstrate that the bicomponent EDIII + NS1 mRNA vaccine combination confers superior protective efficacy compared with either component alone, consistent with a synergistic effect between humoral and cellular immune responses. This study provides a novel strategy for next-generation Zika vaccine development.

abstract: Background: Epithelial-derived carcinomas exhibit genomic instability due to genetic mutation and epigenetic dysregulation. Mechanisms such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and noncoding RNA regulation may lead to tumor progression, immune evasion, and treatment resistance. Presently, gene-based and epigenetic therapies, including CRISPR systems, RNA interference, and chromatin-modifying agents, are reported to be effective in targeted cancer treatment. Objectives: This scoping review aims to map the evidence on gene-based technologies in epithelial-derived carcinomas, including therapeutic, diagnostic, prognostic, screening, and disease-modeling applications, and to identify molecular targets, translational outcomes, and gaps in the current evidence base. The review will characterize the molecular targets, gene-based approaches, cancer types, translational applications, and reported outcomes to identify evidence gaps, translational challenges, and priorities for future research. Methods: The scoping review was conducted as per PRISMA-ScR by conducting a literature search in databases such as PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar, covering studies published between 2016 and 2026. In the inclusion criteria, all studies and reviews related to investigating gene-based, RNA-mediated, and epigenetic therapies in epithelial cancers were included. Thirty-six studies met the eligibility criteria. Results: Amongst the studies reviewed, the most common epithelial cancers reported were hepatocellular carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, lung carcinoma, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Among the epithelial-derived carcinomas identified in this review, HCC was the most frequently represented cancer; epigenetic alterations and therapies used were RNA-based therapies, CRISPR diagnostics, and epigenetic drugs. Ovarian and breast cancers targeting BRCA pathways and chromatin remodeling produced clinical translation outcomes. Lung and colorectal cancers showed moderate epigenetic involvement, often managed through combined therapeutic strategies. Pancreatic cancer therapies were limited by challenges in drug delivery despite identifiable molecular targets. Gene therapies such as CRISPR-based gene editing, RNAi/siRNA therapies, miRNA/lncRNA targeting, and HDAC inhibition were commonly reported. Conclusions: The present study indicates that the majority of epithelial-derived carcinomas can benefit from gene-based and epigenetic therapies. Though the majority of carcinomas, such as hepatocellular, have good clinical outcomes, pancreatic cancer has limited clinical translation.

title: Current Evidence on Gene-Based and Epigenetic Therapeutic, Diagnostic, and Prognostic Strategies in Epithelial-Derived Carcinomas: A Scoping Review.

abstract: Cancer remains a formidable global health challenge, representing the second leading cause of mortality worldwide. In 2023, there were approximately 18.5 million new cancer cases and over 10 million deaths globally, with projections estimating 30.5 million new cases and 18.6 million deaths annually by 2050. In the US, an estimated 2,114,850 new cases and 626,140 deaths are projected for 2026. Cancer arises from accumulated genetic and epigenetic alterations that progressively transform normal cells into malignant counterparts, with mutations in proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair machinery as fundamental drivers of carcinogenesis. Gene therapy has emerged as a therapeutic modality that addresses cancer at its genetic core. This review examines the genetic basis of cancer pathogenesis and analyzes contemporary gene delivery platforms viral vectors, bacterial vectors (bactofection), physical methods (microinjection, electroporation, hydroporation, and gene gun), and chemical approaches (lipofection, polymer based systems, and nanoparticles)alongside their advantages, limitations, and clinical applications. Particular emphasis is placed on suicide gene therapy and immunomodulatory approaches, with focused examination of chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy as the most clinically advanced gene therapy strategy to date. Recent advances, including expanded regulatory designations for CAR-T therapies targeting solid tumors and next-generation vector platforms, underscore the field's rapid evolution. Despite persistent challenges safety concerns, high costs, and limited efficacy in solid tumors, gene therapy represents a transformative approach that may ultimately achieve durable remissions. We conclude by discussing future directions, including next-generation delivery systems, genome editing technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 base and prime editing, and strategies to improve accessibility and affordability.

abstract: Countries with limited water and land resources confront a significant problem due to the growing demand for medicinal plants. These plants are used worldwide to extract and isolate therapeutically important bioactive molecules, known as secondary metabolites. Many medicinal plant species are currently facing significant conservation challenges due to excessive, unregulated harvesting, driven by rapidly growing demand for plant-derived therapies. Soilless farming techniques like hydroponics, aeroponics, and vertical farming offer a sustainable alternative for generating high-quality planting material on a large scale in a considerably shorter period and with less space. Soilless farming revolutionises agriculture and food production, making it particularly well-suited for urban agriculture by reducing maintenance requirements and maximizing crop yields. Soilless farming of numerous medicinal herbs, fruit crops, and vegetables has become increasingly popular in recent years, particularly for its ability to produce large amounts of biomass, high yields, and a wide range of pharmacologically active metabolites. These high-tech systems have significant promise for increased crop yields, cleaner produce, season-independent cultivation, and reduced environmental impact, particularly in water use and disease, compared to traditional soil-based systems. This review article rigorously evaluates recent advancements in soilless agriculture, including LED spectral regulation, nano-elicitation, microbial biostimulants and precursor-feeding strategies, reusable substrates, computational technologies, and CRISPR/Cas-based editing, with respect to their efficacy in generating high-quality plant biomass, improving automation, and optimizing shoot architecture. Implementing soilless farming to produce and synthesize bioactive molecules is expected to be crucial in enhancing sustainability and human well-being.

abstract: Pathogenic variants in SCN1A are associated with a broad and overlapping spectrum of epilepsies, ranging from febrile seizures and genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) to severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs), most notably Dravet syndrome. SCN1A encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunit Nav1.1, which has a critical role in inhibitory interneurons. In classical loss-of-function-associated Dravet syndrome, reduced Nav1.1 function contributes to impaired inhibitory neuronal excitability and network hyperexcitability. However, SCN1A-related disorders are mechanistically heterogeneous, with gain-of-function or mixed-function pathogenic variants being associated with clinically distinct phenotypes, including early-onset DEE and familial hemiplegic migraine type 3 (FHM3). This narrative review integrates functional variant classification with genotype-function-phenotype relationships, clinical diagnosis, and phenotype-specific treatment considerations. Particular emphasis is placed on early molecular testing, careful variant interpretation, and the distinction between chronic sodium-channel-blocker avoidance in classical loss-of-function-associated Dravet syndrome and potential mechanism-informed treatment strategies for selected gain-of-function phenotypes. We also summarize emerging SCN1A-targeted approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide therapy, gene activation, and interneuron-targeted gene replacement. A clearer understanding of variant-specific mechanisms and longitudinal clinical features may improve diagnostic precision, individualized management, and the development of disease-modifying therapies for SCN1A-related epilepsies.

abstract: Inherited anemias represent a diverse group of genetic disorders characterized by impaired red blood cell production, increased destruction, or abnormal hemoglobin synthesis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the contemporary clinical landscape, diagnostic workflows, and therapeutic advancements for both major and rare inherited anemias. Major hemoglobinopathies, including thalassemia and sickle cell disease (SCD), continue to impose a significant global health burden, while rare conditions such as hereditary hemolytic anemias (HHAs), congenital dyserythropoietic anemias (CDAs), and Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) present unique diagnostic challenges. Recent years have seen a paradigm shift in laboratory investigations, primarily driven by the integration of next-generation sequencing (NGS) and third-generation sequencing (TGS) into clinical practice. These technologies have revolutionized the identification of causative variants, particularly in complex or multiallelic cases that elude traditional biochemical assays. Furthermore, specialized flow cytometry, such as eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding, remains critical for the diagnosis of red cell membrane defects. Therapeutic management is also undergoing a transformation. Beyond traditional supportive care and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), groundbreaking gene-editing therapies, most notably CRISPR/Cas9-mediated BCL11A enhancer editing, offer the potential for curative outcomes in beta-hemoglobinopathies. Novel pharmacological agents, such as luspatercept for thalassemia and mitapivat for pyruvate kinase deficiency, are providing targeted options to improve erythropoiesis and reduce transfusion burden. Despite these advances, challenges remain in ensuring equitable access to these high-cost interventions and addressing the diagnostic gaps in resource-limited settings.

abstract: The purpose of this review article is to discuss the current treatment modalities and ongoing clinical trials regarding cardiac amyloidosis (CA), specifically transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrillar proteins. When these proteins are deposited in the heart's myocardium, it is referred to as cardiac amyloidosis. CA can be divided into two main groups: light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL-CA) and transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA), which can be further subdivided into wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRwt) and hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTRv). ATTR-CA is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure in the setting of progressive restrictive cardiomyopathy, particularly among older adults, males, and individuals of African descent, with remarkable advances in the therapeutic landscape. TTR stabilizers, including Tafamidis (approved in 2019) and Acoramidis (approved in 2024), have demonstrated significant reductions in mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations. Gene silencing therapies, including Vutrisiran (approved in 2025), represent a new drug group that targets TTR production at the RNA level. Meanwhile, CRISPR-based gene editing with nexiguran ziclumeran (nex-z or NTLA-2001) and amyloid-depleting monoclonal antibodies offer the prospect of one-time curative treatments and active fibril clearance, respectively. However, despite these advances, substantial knowledge gaps persist: no head-to-head trials have compared stabilizers to silencers, optimal combination therapy regimens remain undefined, and the role of conventional guideline-directed medical therapy in ATTR-CA has only been supported by observational data.

abstract: Short RNA oligonucleotides directed at the 3' splice site region of EGFR exon 3 reduced the proliferation of A172 glioblastoma cells, while the same oligonucleotides had no detectable effect on A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Glioblastoma carries EGFR amplification in roughly a third of IDH-wildtype cases, and the A172 line harbours a tandem duplication in the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain. Because exon definition in human genes depends on RNA-binding proteins that engage exonic sequence near splice sites, we used the SpliceAid database to identify candidate RNA-binding proteins at EGFR exons 2 and 3. Y-box binding protein 1 (YB-1, encoded by YBX1), reported to drive glioblastoma growth through its RNA-binding function, scored highly immediately adjacent to the exon 3 3' splice site. We designed four 2'-modified RNA oligonucleotides carrying a nuclear localisation signal: two antisense oligonucleotides against the exon 3 region (asRNA1, spanning the splice site; asRNA2, downstream of it), a decoy complementary to the asRNA2 target (dRNA2), and a decoy carrying the YB-1 consensus binding sequence (dYB-1). In A172 cells, all four reduced EGFR protein in a single Western blot experiment, and asRNA1, asRNA2 and dRNA2 reduced proliferation relative to scrambled RNA at days 1 to 3; dYB-1 produced a comparable reduction at day 3. None of these effects was seen in A549 cells. YB-1 protein level and subcellular distribution were unchanged by the oligonucleotides, arguing against an indirect route through altered YB-1 abundance. These observations are preliminary. Every experiment reported here was performed once: the proliferation data come from single plates with three wells per group, analysed by Dunnett's test against the scrambled-RNA control, and the Western blot, RT-PCR and immunocytochemistry panels are single runs presented as representative observations. Direct binding of YB-1 to the targeted EGFR sequence has not been demonstrated. We post this work as a preprint so that the design strategy and the initial observations are available while these questions remain open.

abstract: Background/Objectives: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) remains the most aggressive and treatment-refractory primary brain tumor, with current therapeutic modalities providing minimal survival improvement. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapies succeeded in hematologic malignancies but are constrained in solid tumors by tumor heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironment, and delivery challenges. CD276 (B7-H3), a pan-cancer antigen overexpressed in gliomas and correlated with poor patient outcomes, represents a compelling immunotherapeutic target. Methods: Here, we developed a non-viral lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for transient CAR mRNA delivery to T cells and evaluated its application for generating CD276 (B7-H3)-targeted CAR-T cells against GBM. An in-house-assembled T-mixer incorporating polyether ether ketone (PEEK) tubing was integrated with a dual-syringe-pump system for controlled LNP production. Results: LNPs formulated with clinically relevant ionizable lipids, SM-102 and DLin-MC3-DMA, demonstrated high encapsulation efficiency and effective mRNA delivery. Cell-type-dependent expression kinetics were further characterized following LNP-mediated reporter mRNA delivery in K562, NK, NK92, and T cells, revealing differences in transgene expression across cell populations. LNP-mediated delivery of CD276 CAR mRNA enabled generation of CAR-expressing T cells that exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD276-positive LN229 GBM cells in vitro. Conclusions: Collectively, this study demonstrates the feasibility of an adaptable LNP-based platform for non-viral CAR mRNA engineering of T cells and CD276-targeted cytotoxicity against GBM cells in vitro. The combination of transient CAR expression and LNP-mediated mRNA delivery provides a foundation for further optimization and evaluation in preclinical in vivo models.

abstract: In recent years, lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have shown great promise as highly flexible delivery systems for cancer vaccines, which enable effective cargo delivery and allow for controlling their distribution, cell-targeting ability and immunogenicity. Innovations in ionizable lipid chemistry, biodegradable formulations, RNA engineering and LNP design resulted in improvements in RNA encapsulation, endosomal escape, delivery outside the liver, and targeting of lymphoid organs and antigen-presenting cells. All these achievements led to an expansion of strategies for developing cancer vaccines from using only mRNA to personal neoantigen vaccines, self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA (circRNA), peptide/protein vaccines, and multi-purpose platforms that combine antigen delivery and modulation of the immune system. LNPs are also studied as tools for altering the tumor microenvironment (TME) and boosting anti-tumor immunity through local delivery of cytokines and innate immune modulators. Preliminary clinical results with personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines show strong potential for this approach. However, inflammatory toxicity, suitability for repeated dosing, off-target delivery, difficulties with large-scale production, formulation stability, personalized production schedule and regulatory issues are still significant challenges. New biodegradable and PEG-free formulations, innovations in manufacturing and lyophilization technology, and AI-based approaches in lipid screening could help overcome some of these problems.

abstract:
Background:

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis syndrome (WHIMs) is a rare disorder that affects the immune system. People with WHIMs can have severe infections all over their body. WHIMs is caused by a mutation in the CXCR4 gene. Treatment with drugs can help control the infections but does not cure the disorder. Researchers want to try a treatment where they collect stem cells from a person with WHIMS, use base-editing to replace the bad gene with a healthy version, and return the new cells to the person. This could cure WHIMs.

Objective:

To test a treatment using base-edited stem cells in people with WHIMs.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with WHIMs.

Design:

The study has 4 stages.

Stage 1: Screening. Participants will be screened at 1 or more visits. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. A sample of tissue and fluid (biopsy) will be taken from the bone marrow in the hip.

Stage 2: Apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle; the blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Stage 3: Treatment. Participants will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks. They will receive 3 drugs to prepare their body for the procedure. Then the edited stem cells will be returned to their bloodstream. They will stay in the hospital until they recover.

Stage 4: Follow-up. Participants will have 8 follow-up visits over 5 years. Long-term visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) base-edited to repair CXCR4 mutations in 10 participants with (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, and Myelokathexis) WHIM syndrome.

Primary Objective: Evaluate safety of treatment with BE-HSPC CXCR4 in participants with WHIM syndrome.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate:

* Efficacy.
* Genetic correction.
* Immune reconstitution.
* Clinical efficacy.

Exploratory Objective:

Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety assessed by:

* Incidence of adverse events (AEs) for each participant.
* Evaluate overall incidence of AEs for the study.
* Incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs).

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

* Efficacy: \>= 5% gene edited circulating myeloid cells by 12 months after BE HSPC infusion.
* Gene correction:

  --Frequency of corrected alleles in peripheral blood cells (such as myeloid, T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).

  --\>200/microL edited neutrophils by 12 months post receipt of the BE HSPC infusion.
* Immune reconstitution:

  * T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
  * B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
* Clinical efficacy: Improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, wart burden, gastrointestinal complaints, or immune dysregulation.

abstract: Breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy have been overwhelmingly driven by advances in adaptive immunity, leaving the therapeutic potential of innate immunity largely untapped, a gap in the current treatment paradigm. Trained immunity, defined by the durable, mitotically maintained metabolic and epigenetic memory that innate immune cells acquire after transient stimulation, offers a new approach to addressing this deficit. Here we survey the triggering signals, cellular heterogeneity, and molecular circuitry that govern trained immunity within the tumor microenvironment. We dissect its dualistic character: the mechanistic basis by which trained immunity can either restrain or promote tumor progression, and what this ambivalence means for the design of next-generation immunotherapies. These insights inform a growing pipeline of trained-immunity-based cancer vaccines, which we categorize into four engineered platforms, recombinant BCG, β-glucan nanoformulations, lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mRNA bifunctional vaccines, and commensal-derived adjuvants. We further propose that vaccine efficacy may depend in part on host immune context, and outline stratification strategies and dosing schedules that may need to be adjusted according to individual immune status, pending clinical validation. In aggregate, evidence from human bladder cancer, preclinical tumor models, and non-tumor trained immunity studies suggests that trained immunity could elevate innate immunity from a supporting role toward an independent therapeutic axis, although most of its direct cancer applications remain at the preclinical or conceptual stage.

abstract: Reliable circulating biomarkers for prognosis and treatment monitoring in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain limited. Liquid biopsy offers a minimally invasive approach to identify clinically informative tumour-derived markers. Given the emerging role of GalNAc-transferases in cancer biology, we evaluated GALNT13 expression in peripheral blood as a potential biomarker for prognosis and disease monitoring in lung cancer patients. Sensitive molecular assays (nested and digital RT-PCR) were developed to detect GALNT13 mRNA in circulating tumour cells (CTCs). These methods were applied to peripheral blood samples from non-small cell lung cancer patients to assess prognostic value and enable longitudinal monitoring. A cohort of 143 NSCLC patients was analysed, of whom 60% were GALNT13-positive in peripheral blood at baseline. During a five-year follow-up, GALNT13 positivity was significantly associated with reduced overall survival. In several patients, increases in GALNT13 levels preceded radiologic evidence of disease progression. GALNT13 expression in CTCs emerges as a promising biomarker for prognosis and treatment monitoring in NSCLC. Prospective studies in larger cohorts are warranted to validate its clinical utility.
